findings.title: Build executes unpinned remote script fetched with curl | sh
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads and executes whatever content the remote host serves at build time, with no version pin, checksum, or signature verification. The script's content is mutable: anyone who can change what example.com/install.sh returns (domain expiry/renewal, account compromise, upstream breach) gets arbitrary code execution inside the image build and in the resulting image layers. This is a textbook CI/build supply-chain injection surface introduced by this diff (line 3 is new in base..head).

findings.title: curl failure masked by pipe, image builds without the install
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN uses /bin/sh -c, whose pipeline exit status is the last command's (sh), and no pipefail is set. With -s silencing diagnostics and no -f, a failed or HTTP-error download feeds sh an empty/HTML stream: sh exits 0 on empty input, so the build step succeeds and the image ships without whatever install.sh was supposed to install. The error signal (curl's non-zero exit / HTTP status) is discarded at Dockerfile:3 — the build reports success for a failed install, which is silent error loss on a real build path.

findings.title: Build executes unpinned remote script via curl|sh with no integrity check
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 3 (`RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh`) downloads mutable third-party content at build time and executes it as root inside the image build with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no `-f` to reject HTTP error bodies. Whoever controls the script at that URL controls the resulting image (arbitrary code, exfiltration of build secrets, backdoored artifact), and the URL can change contents between builds, so builds are not reproducible. The host is also IANA's reserved documentation domain example.com, which serves no installer — so the line either fetches nothing useful or is a stub pointing at an endpoint that will later be swapped for a live one, the classic supply-chain substitution window.

findings.title: Pipe masks curl failures, so a failed download yields a successful build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL ... | sh` returns the exit status of the last pipeline element (`sh`), not `curl`. If the download fails (DNS outage, network policy, connection refused, 5xx with empty body), curl writes nothing, `sh` reads EOF on an empty script and exits 0, so the build step — and therefore the whole image build — succeeds while silently omitting whatever `install.sh` was supposed to install. `-s` additionally suppresses curl's error messages (and `-f` is absent), so there is no log line either: the failure signal is discarded entirely and downstream consumers (CI, the shipped image, `CMD ["/app"]` runtime) cannot distinguish "installed" from "never ran". This is a silent-error-loss path introduced by this change.

findings.title: Dockerfile pipes unpinned remote script into shell during build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new line `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads whatever that URL serves at build time and executes it as root inside the build container, with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no vendored copy. The endpoint's content can change or be compromised at any time, so every future build silently runs different code — a non-reproducible build and a direct supply-chain compromise path for the produced image. The host is also example.com (a reserved placeholder domain not controlled by this repo), so the executed artifact is entirely third-party and unauthenticated beyond transport TLS.

findings.title: curl failure silently swallowed; build succeeds without running installer
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure): curl's exit status is discarded by the pipeline — Docker runs RUN via /bin/sh -c with no pipefail, so the step's status is sh's, not curl's. Verified directly: `sh -c 'curl -sL https://127.0.0.1:1/nothing | sh'` exits 0 when the download fails entirely (curl fails, sh receives empty input, exits 0), so the image builds 'successfully' with the installer's changes missing. Additionally `-s` without `-f` means an HTTP 404/500 body (e.g. an HTML error page) is piped into sh as if it were the script, and -s suppresses curl's error messages from the build log — failure and success are indistinguishable at the decision point (the build's exit status). downstream, CMD ["/app"] at Dockerfile:5 runs against a filesystem where the install never happened, so any missing dependency surfaces as a runtime failure instead of a failed build.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines deliver results, racing callers that close results
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run blocked until every value was delivered, so the natural caller pattern `worker.Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` (or any sequence that stops reading/tears down after Run returns) was safe: on return, all N sends had completed. After the change, each send happens in a detached goroutine (lines 7-9) with no WaitGroup or other join, so Run returns while sends are still in flight. A caller that closes results after Run returns now hits a nondeterministic `send on closed channel` panic; a caller that stops reading leaves goroutines blocked forever on the send, since the goroutines also never observe ctx (ctx was already unused, but previously the blockage was the caller's own stack frame under its control; now it is an unreachable leak). Either way the completion contract of the exported Run — 'all results emitted when it returns' — no longer holds.

findings.title: Block Run until result sends complete before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (git show cbb8ef3:src/worker.go) Run sent synchronously, so Run returning implied every `results <- j*2` had been delivered, in job order; the canonical usage `results := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` was safe. Lines 7-9 spawn a fire-and-forget goroutine per job, so Run returns with sends still pending: a caller closing results immediately after Run races those sends and Go panics with "send on closed channel" (crash), or a drain `for range results` stops with fewer than len(jobs) values, so downstream code processes partial results as complete. The same change makes sends race each other, so results arrive in nondeterministic order, breaking any positional jobs[i]↔results[i] pairing. The goroutine buys nothing — `j*2` is trivial and the channel already runs producer and receiver concurrently — and no completion signal (WaitGroup/done) or ctx cancellation (ctx at line 5 is still ignored) is provided for callers to synchronize on, so abandoned receivers now leak N goroutines instead of one blocked call.

findings.title: Wait for all sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base revision Run sent every value inline, so on return all results had been received: callers could safely do Run(...); close(results), and a caller reading results positionally got them in jobs order. After this change Run returns immediately after spawning goroutines. With an unbuffered results channel and no receiver running yet, the spawned goroutines are still blocked in 'results <- j*2' when the caller executes close(results), so the senders panic with 'send on closed channel' (crash, not a recoverable error); a caller that zips received values against jobs also gets arbitrary pairing because send order is now scheduler-dependent. The exported completion/ordering contract of Run is removed without any replacement synchronization (no WaitGroup, no done signal) and without documentation.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord || swap allows cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (7e45434) was `return session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId;` — deletion required being an admin OF the record's tenant. Head returns `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId;`, which widens the gate in both dimensions. Substitution 1: session={tenantId:'a', isAdmin:true}, record={tenantId:'b'} → old=false, new=true: an admin of tenant a passes the guard for tenant b's record, a cross-tenant delete bypass; Session carries tenantId precisely to scope admin power and the old code enforced tenant equality even for admins, so there is no global-admin notion that legitimizes this. Substitution 2: session={tenantId:'a', isAdmin:false}, record={tenantId:'a', ownerId:'x'} → old=false, new=true: any same-tenant non-admin now passes, whereas base was admin-only, and record.ownerId is never consulted so the non-admin may delete any record in the tenant. This is an exported public predicate, so the widened authorization contract ships to every caller as-is.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord widened from AND to OR, bypassing tenant isolation
findings.whyItBreaks: The base predicate `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` required BOTH admin status AND tenant match. The head predicate `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` weakens both dimensions: (1) an admin of tenant A now passes for a record in tenant B (`isAdmin=true` short-circuits before the tenant check), so admins can delete other tenants' records — a cross-tenant data-destruction path; (2) a non-admin member of the same tenant now passes (`tenantId === tenantId`), so every ordinary tenant user gains delete rights that previously required admin. Both values substitute directly: session={isAdmin:true, tenantId:'A'} → record.tenantId='B' → old=false, new=true; session={isAdmin:false, tenantId:'A'} → record.tenantId='A' → old=false, new=true. canDeleteRecord is the sole authorization check for record deletion in this repo and is exported as public API, so every eventual caller inherits the bypass.

findings.title: Delete gate widened from isAdmin AND tenant to isAdmin OR tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: Base enforced `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`: only admins could delete, and only inside their own tenant. The new `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` strictly enlarges the accept set in two distinct ways: (1) an admin session now passes for a record in a different tenant (isAdmin=true, session.tenantId=A, record.tenantId=B → previously false, now true), removing the tenant boundary from an admin's delete authority; (2) a non-admin session now passes for any record in its own tenant (isAdmin=false, session.tenantId=A, record.tenantId=A → previously false, now now true), granting delete to users the base explicitly excluded regardless of RecordRef.ownerId, which the predicate never consults. canDeleteRecord is the repo's only delete authorization control and it is exported (public contract), so every consumer of this gate silently inherits the widened authority; cross-tenant delete authorization is a security bypass with data-deletion impact. No test, doc, or call-site in the repo justifies the changed policy.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors; fallback is persisted over real settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The added catch{} (src/settings.ts:14-16) converts every failure — malformed JSON AND the deliberate 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' validation throws (src/settings.ts:11-12) — into a legitimate-looking value. findings.title: pageCount uses Math.floor, dropping the partial last page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount(totalItems, pageSize) must return the number of pages needed to cover every item, which requires rounding up: pageCount(10, 7) was 2 (pages of 7 and 3), but Math.floor(10/7) returns 1, so any consumer iterating pages 0..pageCount-1 never fetches items 8-10 — the final partial page is silently lost. The regression fires on the common case where totalItems % pageSize !== 0 (i.e., most real datasets), and for negative totalItems Math.floor even returns a negative page count (-1 for -1/7) where the previous code returned 0. The function's entire purpose is this ceil-division; no guard or caller compensates for the change.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom with artifacts fetched from a different ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously artifacts came from the same lookup that produced builtFrom: commit = build.ref(branch); artifactsAt(commit). The change adds verified = build.ref("verified") and passes that to artifactsAt while builtFrom still reports commit. For every caller passing a branch other than the literal "verified", build.ref(branch) and build.ref("verified") are two independent lookups that normally yield different commits, so the returned BuildReport claims the build came from commit X while listing commit Y's artifacts — the report's core pairing of builtFrom and artifacts is silently broken, misattributing artifacts (wrong provenance, wrong file lists, downstream consumers trusting builtFrom to describe artifacts).

findings.title: Source report artifacts from the same ref as builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change both fields of BuildReport derived from a single commit: builtFrom: commit and artifacts: build.artifactsAt(commit). The new lines (src/report.ts:13-14) compute commit = build.ref(branch) but pass a different value, verified = build.ref("verified"), to artifactsAt. Whenever the branch ref and the "verified" ref resolve to different commits — the normal case, and the only case in which writing this change makes sense — the returned report claims the artifacts were builtFrom the branch commit while the artifact list actually belongs to the verified commit. Any consumer that renders or acts on "built from <commit>: <artifacts>" (release notes, provenance display, artifact selection keyed off builtFrom) is given misattributed artifacts, and the mismatch is silent: both fields are plain strings with no indication they came from different refs.

findings.title: builtFrom names branch commit, but artifacts come from 'verified' ref
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base (git show 6b8c240:src/report.ts:14) both fields were sourced from the same commit: builtFrom: commit with artifacts: build.artifactsAt(commit), so builtFrom correctly identified the source of artifacts. The new code computes verified = build.ref("verified") (line 13) and passes it to artifactsAt (line 14) while builtFrom still reports build.ref(branch) (lines 12, 14). Whenever the two refs differ — e.g. buildReport(build, "main") while "verified" points at another/lagging commit — the returned BuildReport pairs one commit's provenance with another ref's artifacts. Any consumer that displays, verifies, or reconciles artifacts against builtFrom (checksum match, provenance display, "artifacts present at builtFrom" validation) receives mismatched data: foreign/stale artifacts presented as this branch's build output.

findings.title: Re-apply slice(0, limit) in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old `return [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` was replaced by `if (limit <= 0) return []; return sorted;` — the `.slice(0, limit)` cap is gone. For every limit > 0 the function now returns the entire reversed array, contradicting the doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 ('Returns at most `limit` entries'). Concrete effect on the in-repo caller: renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) calls recentEntries(all, 20) and allocates `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10), then copies `for (i < page.length)` (src/feed.ts:11) — with 50 input entries page.length is now 50, so the copy extends the array past 20 and renderFeed returns 50 entries instead of a 20-entry page. recentEntries is also exported public API, so every external caller passing a limit silently loses the cap.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit` and returns all entries

The doc comment at line 1 promises "Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first", and the only in-repo caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9), calls recentEntries(all, 20) and copies page into a fixed `new Array<string>(20)` (src/feed.ts:10-11). With page.length > 20 the loop writes out[20], out[21], ... past the allocated bound, growing the array, so renderFeed returns the entire history instead of the 20 newest entries — an unbounded, user-facing feed regression. The `if (limit <= 0) return [];` guard does not compensate because it never truncates the positive-limit case.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit) in recentEntries; limit now ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: Base a83cde0 returned `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the head removes the slice, so for any limit > 0 the guard `if (limit <= 0) return []` (line 4) passes through and line 5 returns ALL entries. This violates the function's own contract on line 1 ("Returns at most `limit` entries") and breaks the sole in-repo caller: renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) passes 20, allocates `new Array<string>(20)` (line 10), then copies `page` element-by-element (line 11). Since JS arrays auto-extend, an input of N>20 entries makes renderFeed return an array of length N (e.g. 50 inputs → 50 outputs), so the feed renders the full history instead of a capped 20-entry page — an unbounded, user-facing regression.

findings.title: Manifest entry-count header no longer matches rendered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, rows was entries.map(...) so the invariant 'entry-count == number of data rows' always held (verified via git show 90a8fe8:src/manifest.ts). This diff adds `const live = entries.filter((e) => !e.stale)` and renders rows from `live`, but line 22 still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`. With any stale entry present the emitted manifest declares a count larger than the rows it contains — e.g. entries=[{path:'a',size:1,stale:true}] yields '# entry-count: 1' followed by zero rows. Any consumer that validates the declared count against the row lines (integrity/completeness check) or reads exactly N rows will treat the manifest as truncated or corrupt; with all entries stale it produces a header counting rows that do not exist at all.

findings.title: entry-count header no longer matches rendered rows when stale entries exist
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, rows came from entries.map, so headerLines(opts, entries.length) always equaled the number of emitted rows. The new filter at line 20 drops stale entries from `rows`, but line 22 still passes the unfiltered `entries.length` to headerLines, which emits `# entry-count: ${count}` (src/manifest.ts:15). With one stale entry present the output is internally inconsistent — e.g. `# entry-count: 2` followed by exactly 1 row — so any consumer that validates, iterates, or sizes the manifest from entry-count (the field's sole purpose) gets a count that is wrong by the number of stale entries.

findings.title: Manifest entry-count header includes stale entries while rows exclude them
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `# entry-count: N` always equaled the number of data rows, because both derived from `entries.length`. The PR filters stale entries out of `rows` (lines 20-21) but line 22 still calls `headerLines(opts, entries.length)`. With entries=[{live},{stale}] the output is `# entry-count: 2` followed by exactly one row. Any consumer that parses entry-count to know how many rows to expect (completeness/integrity check, pre-sizing, iteration bound) sees an over-count and either reports corruption or reads past the end of the data. The count and rows are produced by adjacent lines of the same expression, so their divergence is a defect in the emitted artifact itself, not a matter of downstream interpretation.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against latest while fromRevision reports pinnedTag

findings.title: Await between stock check and update lets concurrent reserves oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff `reserve` was synchronous, so guard (`remaining <= 0`, line 16) and write (`stock.set`, line 18) executed atomically within one JS turn and could never interleave. The added `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) yields between the read (line 15) and the write (line 18). With stock=1, call A reads 1, passes the guard, suspends at the await; call B then reads the still-unchanged 1, passes the guard, suspends; both resume and both write `remaining - 1 = 0` and both return true — two successful reservations from one unit (and the persisted count is written twice with the same stale value, never reflecting two decrements). With stock=2, A and B each write 1 instead of 0 — a lost decrement that lets a third reservation succeed, compounding the oversell. `reserve` becoming async (line 14) is precisely what makes overlapping invocations possible.

findings.title: reserve() check-then-act spans an await; concurrent calls oversell stock
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads stock and passes the `remaining <= 0` guard (src/inventory.ts:15-16), then newly suspends at `await this.store.save(...)` (src/inventory.ts:17) before mutating `this.stock` (src/inventory.ts:18). The pre-diff synchronous body ran check and update in one atomic synchronous block; the added await yields to the event loop in between, so a second reserve() invoked before the first resumes re-reads the same stale `remaining`, also passes the guard, and also returns true. With stock=1, `Promise.all([inv.reserve(sku), inv.reserve(sku)])` resolves [true, true] — two reservations for one unit; with stock=N both calls persist the same stale `remaining - 1`, so the persisted count is wrong as well.

findings.title: reserve() check-then-act race across await allows oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR reserve() was fully synchronous and therefore atomic under JS's single-threaded execution: the guard (remaining <= 0) and the decrement were one uninterruptible step. The new async body reads this.stock at line 15, passes the guard at line 16, then yields at `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17) before committing the decrement at line 18. Any second reserve() call for the same SKU invoked before that continuation resumes (the normal case: Promise.all / concurrent requests, since the async API invites concurrent awaiting) reads the same stale `remaining`, passes the same guard, persists the same value, and also returns true. Concrete trace with load('A', 1): call A reads remaining=1, suspends at line 17; call B runs synchronously, reads remaining=1 (stock not yet updated), suspends at line 17; A resumes, sets stock=0, returns true; B resumes, sets stock=0, returns true. Result: 2 units reserved from 1 unit of stock, store persisted twice with 0 — the guard's entire purpose (block reservation when no stock remains) is bypassed. This holds even if save() resolves instantly, because await always defers the continuation past the caller's subsequent synchronous reserve() invocation.

findings.title: Make retry() stop multiplying the now-millisecond backoff by 1000
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds (min(30, 2**attempt)); it now returns milliseconds (min(30_000, 2**attempt * 1000)). src/net/poll.ts was updated for the new unit, but the other consumer, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)` where sleep takes ms. After this change retry's first failure sleeps 1*1000*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min, was 1s) and the cap becomes 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000 ms (~8.3h, was 30s). retry() is an exported public API, so any job using it appears hung for minutes-to-hours after a single transient failure.

findings.title: Propagate file close error in store.Save instead of discarding
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (902d663) ended the success path with `return f.Close()`, propagating the os.File.Close error to the caller. Head (77c2ed9) uses `defer f.Close()` at store/save.go:13 and returns only `w.Flush()`, discarding the close error. bufio.Flush only reports errors from the writes it performs; os.File.Close can still fail afterwards (write-behind/NFS/Windows close errors, delayed writeback), and that failure now yields Save(...) == nil. Because store.Save is an exported API, every caller is forced to conflate 'failed close' (possible truncated/undurable file) with a successful save — a TRIGGER D public-contract defect even though nothing in this repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Save silently swallows f.Close() error that base returned to callers

The head replaces this with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) whose return value is discarded, and `return w.Flush()` (line 20), so on the success path Save now returns nil when Close fails. Callers can no longer distinguish 'persisted' from 'close failed' and will report/report-on data as saved when it may not be. Save is the package's only exported symbol, so this forces every eventual caller to conflate failure with success even though nothing in this repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Save swallows file Close error, reporting failed writes as success

findings.title: page_window off-by-one drops the last row of every page
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop was changed from range(start, end) to range(start, end - 1), so the half-open bounds computed by _window_bounds (correct: end is exclusive, min(start+page_size, row_count)) are then treated as inclusive. Every page loses its final row: for rows=['a','b','c'], page_index=0, page_size=3, _window_bounds returns (0,3) but page_window returns ['a','b'], so render_page emits only '1. a\n2. b' (the '3. c' line vanishes) and summarize drops exactly one row per page. The new docstring "Rows belonging to page_index" promises the full window, but the body computes rows[start:end-1]. This is introduced by this PR (base at 3f7eaeb used range(start, end)).

findings.title: Restore TtlCache.get TTL comparison; it now serves expired entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (161224c0) checked `Date.now() - entry.storedAt < this.ttlMs` (fresh → return value). The PR flips it to `>`. Substituting values: a fresh entry (age=0, ttl=50) fails the `>` guard, falls through to line 21 delete + line 22 return null — every within-TTL read destroys the entry and misses, so the cache can never serve a fresh value. An expired entry (age=100, ttl=50) passes the guard and returns entry.value at line 19 without ever being deleted, so expired values are returned indefinitely and leak in the Map. Cache semantics are fully inverted on both branches: fresh→miss+evict, expired→hit+leak.

findings.title: Fix pruneDone: splice during forEach leaks done jobs and mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: Base (161224c0) was `return jobs.filter((job) => !job.done)` — returns a fresh array, caller's input untouched. The PR mutates `jobs` with `jobs.splice(index, 1)` inside `forEach`: after a splice the array shifts left while forEach still advances its index, so the element immediately after a removed done job is never inspected. Substitution: jobs=[A(done),B(done),C(pending)] → splice(0) yields [B,C], forEach advances to index1=C, B is skipped → returns [B,C] with a done job still queued; jobs=[A(pending),B(done),C(done)] → splice(1) yields [A,C], forEach ends → returns [A,C]. Two adjacent done jobs (the common case when multiple jobs complete between prunes) survive pruning and would be reprocessed. Additionally the function now returns the same array reference and mutates the caller's array mid-iteration (base returned a copy), so callers holding `jobs` observe entries vanishing.

findings.title: TtlCache.get TTL check inverted: serves expired, evicts fresh
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `<` to `>`. storedAt is set to Date.now() on set() (src/cache.ts:12), so `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs` is true only when the entry is EXPIRED. Consequences: a fresh entry (age <= ttl) falls through to entries.delete(key) and returns null, so the cache never reports a hit within its TTL; an expired entry (age > ttl) returns entry.value, so stale data is served indefinitely and is never evicted. Every consumer of get() observes exactly backwards TTL behavior.

findings.title: pruneDone skips consecutive done jobs by splicing during forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing at the current index while forEach advances by index skips the element that shifts into the vacated slot. Trace with jobs=[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]: index 0 is done -> splice(0,1) -> array becomes [{done:true},{done:false}]; forEach then probes index 1, which is now the not-done job, so the second done job is never examined and remains in the result. pruneDone therefore returns arrays still containing done jobs, and any downstream consumer will re-process work already marked complete. The original `jobs.filter((job) => !job.done)` had no such defect.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation used Array.prototype.filter, which returns a new array and leaves the input untouched. The new implementation removes elements from the caller's own array via jobs.splice, so any caller that retains a reference to the passed array (shared queue state, a list being rendered, a second consumer iterating the same array) observes elements disappearing as a side effect of a function whose name and return value suggest a pure transform. This is an in-place mutation of caller data introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL comparison in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing '<' to '>' at src/cache.ts:18 inverts TTL semantics. A fresh entry (age < ttlMs) takes the false branch, is deleted at src/cache.ts:21, and get() returns null — so set() followed by get() within the TTL never returns the cached value and destroys the entry. An expired entry (age > ttlMs) takes the true branch and is returned at src/cache.ts:19 on every subsequent call and is never evicted, so stale data is served past its TTL indefinitely. The two branches are internally incoherent with the delete+null fallthrough at lines 21-22, which only makes sense for expired entries. Every input state now behaves opposite to the contract implied by ttlMs.

findings.title: Fix pruneDone splice-during-forEach: skips jobs, mutates input
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach visits by index while splice shifts elements left (src/queue.ts:7-11). For jobs=[doneA, doneB, pendingC]: index0 removes doneA leaving [doneB, pendingC]; forEach then visits index1, which is now pendingC, and index2 no longer exists — doneB survives in the returned array. pruneDone([done, done]) returns [done]: with all jobs done the function fails its sole purpose, and any run of two or more adjacent completed jobs leaks done jobs back to callers, which can reprocess already-completed work. Additionally, splice mutates the caller's array in place, whereas the previous `jobs.filter` (base src/queue.ts:7) returned a new array — any caller still holding the original reference now observes it shrinking.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy so busiest() stops mutating caller input
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates its receiver and returns the same reference, so `rows.sort(...)` at src/stats.ts:12 reorders the caller-owned array as a side effect. The base version (af2477c) sorted a `[...rows]` copy and was non-mutating; any caller that passes an array and later reads it (rendering original order, iterating twice, sharing the array with averageAmount) now silently observes descending-amount order. The function reads as a pure query but now has an undocumented order-changing side effect on caller data.

findings.title: Guard empty input in averageAmount to stop returning NaN

Now rows.reduce(..., 0) yields 0 and 0/0 evaluates to NaN, so every empty-input call receives a non-numeric result: JSON.stringify serializes it as null and any comparison (avg > threshold, avg === 0) is silently false — a wrong persisted/reported value with no error raised.

findings.title: Sort a copy in busiest so caller arrays are not reordered
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort reorders the receiver in place and returns the same reference; the previous `[...rows]` copy isolated the caller. busiest() now rewrites the caller-owned array into descending-amount order as a side effect, so any caller that iterates, renders, or persists its rows after calling busiest(rows) observes them silently reordered (the returned element is unchanged, which hides the side effect).

findings.title: Guard averageAmount against empty input to avoid NaN

An empty dataset is a normal input for a stats helper, and NaN fails every numeric comparison (isNaN checks absent), silently propagates through arithmetic, and serializes as null via JSON.stringify — so any caller persisting or displaying the result reports wrong data with no error.

findings.title: Restore defensive copy so busiest does not mutate caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR replaces `[...rows].sort(...)` with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place and returns the same array, so busiest() now silently reorders the caller-owned input as a side effect. A caller that renders or persists rows in their original order, or shares the array across components/requests, gets its data rewritten into descending-amount order merely by asking which row is busiest — a dropped defensive copy with caller-visible data mutation.

findings.title: scores.sort() without comparator sorts lexicographically, breaking topPlayers cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) (numeric descending). The new rankScores uses bare scores.sort(), which converts numbers to strings and orders by UTF-16 code units, then reverses. For scores [10, 9, 100] the result is [9, 100, 10] instead of [100, 10, 9], so with n=2 the cutoff at src/leaderboard.ts:15 becomes scores[1]=100; the filter at line 16 then returns only the 100-point player (slice(0,2) never reached), whereas the correct result is the two players with 100 and 10. Same defect for negatives ([-1,-2,-10] → [-2,-10,-1]). formatBoard (src/leaderboard.ts:19-23) renders this wrong ranking directly to the user. Carrier enumeration (Trigger C): carrier=topPlayers @src/leaderboard.ts:13 promises=top n players by score; body=scores.sort() lexicographic + reverse @src/leaderboard.ts:8-9; caller=formatBoard @src/leaderboard.ts:20 relies=yes.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically in rankScores, not lexicographically
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaced `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` with `scores.sort()` + `scores.reverse()`. Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator orders by string code units, not numerically, so any scores with differing digit counts (>=10, negatives, decimals) are misordered: for scores [100, 5] it yields [5, 100] after reverse. topPlayers then reads `cutoff = scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` (src/leaderboard.ts:15), so with players [{a,5},{b,100}] and n=1 the cutoff becomes 5 instead of 100; `players.filter(p => p.score >= cutoff).slice(0, n)` (line 16) keeps both players and returns the first input element — player a with score 5 — instead of the actual top scorer. Verified by executing the exact logic: input [{a,5},{b,100}], n=1 → [{name:"a",score:5}]. The previously working path (base commit used the numeric comparator) is a direct regression, and formatBoard (line 20) inherits the wrong ranking in its numbered output.

findings.title: Default sort ranks scores lexicographically, returning wrong top players
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() with no comparator coerces each number to a string, so [5,45,100] sorts to ['100','45','5'] ascending and, after reverse(), to [5,45,100] — not numerically descending. topPlayers then takes cutoff = scores[min(n,len)-1]; for n=1 that is 5 instead of 100, the filter p.score >= 5 admits every player, and slice(0,n) returns the first player in input order — the lowest scorer is reported as rank 1. Verified by substituting the values: scores=[5,45,100] -> cutoff=5 -> result=[{name:'a',score:5}] instead of {name:'c',score:100}. The pre-PR code sorted with (a,b)=>b-a (numeric descending), so this is a user-facing regression in both topPlayers and its caller formatBoard. Any multi-digit or mixed-magnitude scores produce wrong leaderboard output.

findings.title: Webhook signature verify downgraded from constant-time to ==
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously compared expected vs given signatures with hmac.compare_digest (line 10 before the diff), which is constant-time by contract. The new `signature_of(...) == given_signature` uses CPython's generic string equality, which short-circuits on the first differing character, so comparison time leaks prefix information about the expected HMAC. An attacker who can measure response times for many forged signatures on handle()'s auth gate (app/webhook.py:13-15, which returns 401 vs 200 based on this result) can progressively recover a valid signature and forge webhook requests. This is a straightforward reversal of the standard hmac verification pattern with no compensating mitigation anywhere in the repo.

findings.title: Webhook signature check uses `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the authentication gate for incoming webhook payloads (handle() at line 14 rejects with 401 when it fails). Replacing hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` makes the comparison short-circuiting rather than constant-time, leaking prefix-match information about the valid HMAC through response timing. An attacker can recover a valid signature byte-by-byte via timing measurements and then forge webhooks that pass verification, since a correct hexdigest match fully authenticates the payload. This is a security regression: the previous line already used the correct constant-time primitive.

findings.title: Webhook signature check uses non-constant-time == instead of compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates webhook payloads: handle() (app/webhook.py:14) gates a 401 vs. executing processor(payload) on its result, so this comparison is the sole authentication boundary. The previous code used hmac.compare_digest, which compares in time independent of the content of the digests; the new code uses Python's == on hexdigest strings, which short-circuits on the first differing character/length. An attacker who can measure response times can recover the expected HMAC one byte at a time and forge valid signatures for arbitrary payloads (security bypass of webhook authentication). The change removes the exact protection compare_digest exists to provide, with no compensating control anywhere in the repo.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base version all three statements (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) executed inside `with db.transaction():`, so they committed or rolled back as one unit. After this change the ledger INSERT commits when the with-block exits (line 22-23) and `_apply_balances` runs afterward, outside that transaction (line 24). Any failure between the debit and the credit (DB error, connection drop, disk error) now persists state the old code rolled back: a committed ledger row claiming the transfer happened plus a debit applied to the source with no credit to the destination — funds are destroyed and the ledger no longer reconciles with balances. Even with no failure, a concurrent reader can observe the committed ledger row before balances change, a write-visibility anomaly that did not exist before. The refactor gains nothing: the helper split is compatible with keeping both calls inside the `with` block.

findings.title: Move balance updates back inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base commit all three statements (ledger INSERT + debit UPDATE + credit UPDATE) ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so a transfer committed or rolled back as one unit. The head commit calls `_record_ledger` inside the block (line 23) but calls `_apply_balances` after the block exits (line 24), so the ledger insert is committed before any balance changes and the two UPDATEs run in their own transaction(s). Concrete failures: (1) if the credit UPDATE raises after the debit UPDATE succeeded, `cents` is destroyed — total balances drop by cents while the committed ledger still claims the money moved; (2) if either UPDATE fails, the ledger row is already committed and can never roll back, so the ledger records a transfer the balances never reflect; (3) even on the success path there is a committed window where readers/reconciliation see a ledger entry with unchanged balances. The double-entry invariant (sum(ledger) == delta of sum(accounts)) no longer holds on any failure path.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local time, silently dropping UTC determinism
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version (345defd) computed the day via getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so the same instant always produced the same 'YYYY-MM-DD' regardless of environment. Head (ad7e559) line 4 uses at.getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate(), which apply the host's local UTC offset. For an instant near a day boundary, e.g. new Date('2026-01-01T00:30:00Z'), a process with TZ=America/New_York yields '2025-12-31' while TZ=UTC yields '2026-01-01'. In a billing surface this means day bucketing differs across fleet members with different TZ settings, and existing persisted/computed UTC-based billing days stop matching newly computed ones on upgrade (silent misclassification of usage/invoice days). sameBillingDay (lines 7-9) inherits the same shift, so two instants on the same UTC day can compare unequal. Nothing in the diff (no comment, doc, or test) indicates the UTC-to-local contract change was intended.

findings.title: Restore UTC date fields in billingDay or justify timezone change
findings.whyItBreaks: The hunk replaced getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate with getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. On any host not running in UTC, an instant near UTC midnight now formats to a different calendar day: e.g. new Date('2026-09-23T20:00:00Z') produced '2026-09-23' before and produces '2026-09-24' under TZ=Asia/Tokyo now. billingDay output therefore depends on the machine's timezone (nondeterministic across deploys/CI), and newly computed day strings no longer align with days previously persisted under the UTC basis, so sameBillingDay (line 8) comparisons against historical values can mis-bucket charges. The rest of the diff — the pad() helper and array join — is purely cosmetic and reproduces the old 'YYYY-MM-DD' format exactly, indicating the UTC→local swap was accidental, not an intended semantics change.

findings.title: Billing day computed in local time, regressing from UTC bucketing
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version deliberately used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so billingDay returned a canonical UTC day regardless of where the process runs. The new line uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the same Date maps to a different billing day depending on the host TZ and DST: e.g. new Date('2026-09-23T01:00:00Z') returned '2026-09-23' before, but returns '2026-09-22' under TZ=America/New_York (and near year boundaries the year itself differs, e.g. '2026-01-01' vs '2025-12-31'). Consequences: (1) records persisted under the old UTC-derived day keys no longer compare equal to newly computed keys, so sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:8) and any daily/monthly billing cutoff split or merge incorrectly; (2) results drift between environments (tests on UTC hosts pass, servers with a local TZ mis-bucket revenue across day/month boundaries). The diff changes silent, environment-dependent billing semantics with no stated intent, doc, or test covering it.

findings.title: Profile cache key omits tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a module-level Map shared by every call (src/profile.ts:7). Precondition substitution: tenant='t2', account='acct' after tenant='t1', account='acct' was cached → key='acct' → memo.get('acct') hits at line 15 → `if (cached) return cached` at line 16 returns t1's Profile (including its tenant/displayName fields) for the t2 request, and fetchProfile('t2','acct') is never called. Account identifiers are per-tenant values that routinely collide across tenants, so any caller reading profiles for more than one tenant gets another tenant's data — both a wrong result and a cross-tenant disclosure. Before this change the key `${tenant}:${account}` kept tenants isolated.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, returning cross-tenant cached profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level memo Map (src/profile.ts:7) is now keyed by account alone (line 14: const key = account). fetchProfile is tenant-dependent — it takes tenant as an argument (line 12, 17) and Profile carries tenant (line 2). Substitution performed: call readProfile('t1','acct',f) caches under 'acct' (line 18); a subsequent readProfile('t2','acct',f) hits memo.get('acct') at line 15, returns at line 16 the profile fetched for tenant 't1', and never invokes fetchProfile for 't2'. The caller receives a Profile whose tenant and displayName belong to a different tenant — wrong data served and cross-tenant profile leakage for any caller that resolves the same account name under two tenants. Before this change the key `${tenant}:${account}` isolated the caches per tenant.

findings.title: Cache key omits tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo cache key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to just `account` (line 14). The cache `memo` (line 7) is module-global and unbounded. Sequence: caller A invokes readProfile('tenant-1', 'acct-42', fetch) → miss → fetchProfile('tenant-1','acct-42') returns {tenant:'tenant-1', account:'acct-42', displayName:'Alice'} → memo.set('acct-42', ...). Later, caller B invokes readProfile('tenant-2', 'acct-42', fetch) → memo.get('acct-42') hits (line 15) → returns tenant-1's Profile (line 16) without ever calling fetchProfile for tenant-2. Account identifiers are only unique per-tenant, so any two tenants sharing an account id cross-contaminate: wrong displayName/tenant attribution and cross-tenant disclosure of profile data. Because `tenant` is still a parameter and is still passed to fetchProfile (line 17), the bug is silent — no error surfaces.

findings.title: Catch-all in load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch added around load()'s body catches the Error thrown for a missing key (line 4) and returns "" instead of propagating it. Previously the throw reached every caller (base version, verified with git show b68a38f:src/store.ts: threw `missing: ${key}`); now failure and a stored empty string are identical at every decision point. In-repo relying consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:11-12) regresses concretely: loadAll(['k'], new Map()) used to throw `missing: k`, now returns [""], so downstream code can persist, report, or act on a default as if it were real data. The catch is also a catch-all: it equally swallows unexpected TypeErrors (e.g. a non-Map `store` where `store.get` is not a function), turning a loud programming error into a silent "". `load` is an exported/public symbol, so the broken contract (errors no longer observable) is the defect regardless of caller count.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent, and that error propagated to every caller — including loadAll (src/store.ts:12) and any external consumer of this exported function. The new try/catch wraps the only throw in the body (Map.get itself cannot throw), so the catch exists solely to convert the missing-key failure into "". A caller can no longer distinguish "key absent" from "key present with value "": code that relied on catching the error to handle absence now silently receives a default, and loadAll now returns [""] for absent keys instead of failing loudly. Failure and fallback value are conflated at every decision point.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and silently returns ""
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the undefined check at src/store.ts:4 threw, and that error propagated to the caller, making 'key absent' unambiguously detectable. The new catch block at src/store.ts:6-8 intercepts exactly that throw (store.get on a Map does not otherwise throw, so the catch exists solely to swallow the missing-key error) and returns "". Because "" is also a valid stored value, every consumer must now treat a missing key and an empty value identically. This is an exported/public contract: both load (src/store.ts:1) and loadAll (src/store.ts:11-12, which maps load over every key) now silently emit "" entries instead of failing, so any caller performing lookups, validation, or persistence through either function gets a fallback it cannot distinguish from real data. Per the swallow-error rule, an exported swallow site is a present defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Remove duplicate retryBackground or implement background execution
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (src/retry.ts:20-31) reimplements the existing retry (src/retry.ts:7-18) with a byte-identical body except the loop bound reads config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts. Because Config requires BOTH bounds (src/retry.ts:2-3), retry(fn, {maxAttempts: N, retries: N, timeout}) produces exactly the behavior of retryBackground(fn, {retries: N, ...}) — the new export adds no capability, only a second identical path to maintain. The name also promises background/deferred execution, yet the body invokes fn synchronously on the caller's thread (src/retry.ts:24-26); a caller choosing it for non-blocking work gets blocking inline work.

findings.title: Make retries mean post-first attempts so retries:0 still runs fn
findings.whyItBreaks: The carrier retries (src/retry.ts:3) coexists with maxAttempts (src/retry.ts:2) on the same required Config, implying retries = additional attempts after the first; the body (src/retry.ts:22) instead uses it as the TOTAL attempt cap. Substituting the natural sentinel retries=0: guard `i < config.retries` @ src/retry.ts:22 is false on entry, the loop never runs, fn is never invoked, and the function returns void — the requested background work is silently, wholly skipped with no error. retries=N yields N invocations rather than the 1+N the field name promises. Attempt count is caller-observable capping behavior of an exported API, so the promise itself is the contract.

findings.title: Propagate final error when retryBackground exhausts retries
findings.whyItBreaks: The added catch-all (src/retry.ts:27-28) discards every exception from fn, and both exit paths — deadline return (src/retry.ts:23) and normal loop completion (src/retry.ts:30-31) — return void with no signal. A caller of this exported function cannot distinguish 'operation succeeded' from 'every attempt threw' or 'zero attempts ran', so it will treat a totally failed operation as done and persist/report that normal return as real success. This is a public swallow site: the contract forces every eventual caller to conflate failure with a legitimate value, and the failure is neither logged nor distinguishable at any decision point.

findings.title: Stop echoing the deploy secret value to the CI log
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step loads `secrets.TOKEN` into the shell environment and writes its raw value to the step's stdout (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`), which is the workflow job log. The line has no functional effect on the deploy (it does not feed `make build`, which is a separate step with no TOKEN env), so its only observable output is a credential in logs. The only barrier against exposure is GitHub's automatic log masking of registered secrets; that masking is a downstream safety net, not a handling guarantee (it does not protect the value if it is transformed/split before printing or if the log is consumed by tooling that sees pre-mask output), and handling a deploy token this way is exactly the pattern secret-scanning and CI security review flag on a `on: push` workflow that runs for every push.

findings.title: Workflow echoes deploy secret TOKEN into job logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step binds the live deploy credential to the shell environment (TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}) and its only command is `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, so the sole observable effect of the step is expanding a secret into the job's stdout. rg over the repo shows TOKEN has no other consumer and the step performs no deployment action, so the credential is placed on the log disclosure path with no compensating benefit. Disclosure prevention rests entirely on GitHub's exact-string log masking (a platform mitigation, not anything enforced by this workflow); any path where the value is not the exact registered string, or where step output is consumed outside GitHub's masked log pipeline, discloses the raw deploy token to everyone with log/diagnostic access.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git() so >1 MiB diffs don't abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. With the explicit 64 MiB cap removed, any git() call whose stdout exceeds 1 MiB is terminated (verified on Node v24: status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error=ENOBUFS). git() at line 38 then evaluates null !== 0 and throws with an empty stderr message; runGithub's catch (lines 182-193) posts a failing 'Needlefish: review failed' check and sets exit code 1, so the PR receives no review. The main producer, `git diff mergeBase headSha` at line 140 (the full unified patch), exceeds 1 MiB for ordinary large PRs (lockfile bumps, generated code, renames — a single pnpm-lock.yaml diff is routinely multi-MB), where the pre-change code handled up to 64 MiB. The sibling gh/ghText helpers (lines 19, 29) kept the 64 MiB cap, showing the removal from git() is an accidental capacity regression, not a coordinated policy change.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer: default 1 MiB cap breaks large patches
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 from git()'s spawnSync options. Node's spawnSync default is 1 MiB; I verified with the same mechanism that a child writing ~2 MiB to stdout returns status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error=ENOBUFS with stdout truncated at ~1049580 bytes. git() only checks res.status !== 0 (line 38), so it throws `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha> failed: ` with empty stderr — the ENOBUFS root cause is dropped from the message. The primary consumer is line 140 `const patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha])`, which produces the entire PR patch with no size bound; any PR whose textual diff exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated assets, large PRs) previously succeeded under the 64 MiB cap and now throws. That throw happens at line 140, before the try block at line 176, so neither the review nor the 'Needlefish: review failed' check is posted and the run aborts with no indication the cause was buffer exhaustion. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers still set 64 MiB (lines 19 and 29), so the removal looks accidental rather than a deliberate policy.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only`: spawned codex can now write to the workspace
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 20 previously passed `-s read-only`, a CLI override that (verified in codex-cli 0.155.1 source) wins over all config: exec/src/lib.rs:328-331 turns the flag into `sandbox_mode = Some(ReadOnly)`, and config/src/config_toml.rs:806 `configured_sandbox_mode = sandbox_mode_override.or(self.sandbox_mode)` therefore forces `PermissionProfile::read_only()` (config_toml.rs:822-824) no matter what config.toml or the project says. After this diff `sandbox_mode` is `None`, so resolution falls through: config `sandbox_mode` if set (valid values include workspace-write and danger-full-access, config_toml.rs:806), else — when the target repo has a recorded trust decision — `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` (config_toml.rs:807-813), else default ReadOnly (config_toml.rs:814 + `#[default] ReadOnly` in protocol/src/config_types.rs:104-112). Concrete wrong behavior: `runCodex` spawns codex with cwd=opts.repoPath (line 24) and feeds a caller-supplied prompt on stdin (line 25); on any machine where the repo is trust-recorded in ~/.codex/config.toml, or config sets `sandbox_mode`, or a trusted project-local `.codex/config.toml` sets it (sandbox_mode is not in the project-config ignore list), model-generated shell commands now write files in the workspace — or run with no filesystem/network boundary under danger-full-access — where the code previously guaranteed read-only. Prompt-injected instructions in the (typically untrusted, e.g. PR-derived) prompt can therefore mutate the reviewed repo or host.

findings.title: Use merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha for patch, not baseSha..HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines computed merge-base(baseSha, headSha), which by construction yields only PR changes. Line 139 now runs `git diff baseSha HEAD`: (1) when PR_BASE_SHA (line 138) is the base-branch tip and is NOT an ancestor of local HEAD (base advanced past the branch point while HEAD is the PR head — the normal head-checkout case), the two-dot diff emits every base-only commit in reverse, so `patch` shows changes the PR never made and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) at line 140 lists base-only files as PR-changed; those paths flow into changedPaths (line 141), pass the inlineComments filter (line 63), and make the POST /pulls/N/reviews call reject phantom paths (422), after which the fallback (lines 96-108) posts the review with ALL inline comments silently dropped. (2) Line 139 now hardcodes HEAD while PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137) is still reported as bundle.headSha (line 165) and posted as commit_id/head_sha (lines 85, 124, 178-179): whenever PR_HEAD_SHA differs from local HEAD (default Actions merge-ref checkout), the patch and comment line numbers are derived from HEAD's tree but GitHub validates them against headSha's diff, so inline comments are rejected or anchored to wrong lines and the review body describes a different commit than the reported head. The env-override path is exactly what lines 137-138 exist for; the old code defended it, the new code does not.

findings.title: Drop merge-base normalization: two-dot diff includes base-only changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines computed `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` first, which is a no-op when baseSha is already the fork point but correct when it is not. PR_BASE_SHA is populated from the pull_request payload, where base.sha is the base-branch tip; once the base branch advances past the PR's fork point (any merge to main after the PR opened), `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 139) and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (line 140, which diffs `baseSha..HEAD` at line 57) present base-side commits as PR changes — files the PR never touched appear modified/deleted in bundle.patch. The reviewer then evaluates phantom hunks and can return the wrong verdict (e.g. REQUEST_CHANGES for a 'deletion' the PR never made). Additionally, changedPaths grows with non-PR files, so inlineComments (lines 61-63) can emit comments on paths GitHub does not consider part of the PR diff; GitHub rejects such review comments with 422, and the postReview fallback (lines 96-108) then drops ALL inline comments, not just the invalid ones. The default no-env path (baseSha already a merge-base) is unaffected, which is why the regression hides under local runs.

findings.title: Patch diffed against HEAD while headSha drives check and review posting
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the patch was `diff mergeBase headSha`, consistent with bundle.headSha (line 165), review commit_id (lines 85/178) and check-run head_sha (lines 124/179), all of which still come from PR_HEAD_SHA (line 137). Line 139 now diffs to the literal `HEAD`, so whenever PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD (e.g. a workflow that checks out the base branch or the refs/pull/N/merge commit while exporting PR_HEAD_SHA), the patch the reviewer analyzes describes a different commit than the one the check-run and inline comments are attached to. In the extreme case (HEAD equals the base tip, as with a default pull_request_target checkout), the diff is empty, the review vacuously passes, and a 'success' check is posted to the PR head that was never reviewed; at minimum, inline comment line numbers computed from HEAD's diff are rendered by GitHub against headSha, yielding wrong-line or rejected comments.

findings.title: Restore function replacers: raw strings expand $&, $$, $' and $` in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only skips ECMAScript $-substitution when the replacer is a function; with a string replacer, GetSubstitution rewrites $$->`$`, $&->the matched token, $`->the text before the match, and $'->the text after the match. The base commit used `() => ...` at all three sites (lines 25, 32, 33), which inserted the JSON/patch verbatim. After this diff: (a) line 33 — a patch containing `$$` (ubiquitous in Makefile/shell hunks) is silently rewritten to `$`, so the critic reviews a patch that differs from the real diff; a patch containing `$&` gets the literal `{{PATCH}}` placeholder injected; `$'` or a `$`+backtick sequence splices the entire tail/prefix of critic.md into the middle of the patch, corrupting the prompt and typically making extractJson fail; (b) lines 25 and 32 — the same substitutions corrupt the JSON-serialized bundle/findings, where $' or $-backtick duplication breaks the JSON structure the model is asked to parse. Verified directly with node: string replacer produced `Xcosts $5 and {{PATCH}} and <suffix> and <prefix>Y` from input containing `$$ $& $' $`` while the function replacer preserved it verbatim.

findings.title: String replacer expands `$` patterns, corrupting injected patch and JSON
findings.whyItBreaks:
Base (05099fa) used function replacers — `() => JSON.stringify(...)` and `() => bundle.patch` — which insert the value literally. The head (cf59c88) passes the values directly as strings (lines 25, 32, 33). For a string second argument, String.prototype.replace interprets `$&` (inserts the matched `{{PATCH}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}` text), `` $` `` (inserts the entire prompt prefix before the placeholder), `$'` (inserts the entire prompt suffix), and `$$` (collapses to a single `$`). `bundle.patch` is arbitrary repository diff text and the bundle/findings JSON embeds it verbatim (JSON.stringify does not escape `$`), so common content such as shell/Makefile `$$`, bash `$'...'`, a JS `.replace(x, "$&")`, or a template-literal `` $` `` in the diff mangles the prompt: patch bytes are altered or template text is injected mid-patch. The critic at line 34 then reviews corrupted input, yielding wrong or missing findings; with `` $` ``/`$'` the prompt duplicates large template regions, materially changing what the model sees. Verified by executing equivalent JS: the string form produced `HEAD
a 
TAIL b
TAIL` for a `$'` value while the function form preserved `$' $& $1` exactly.

findings.title: Restore callback replacer so $ patterns in patch are not expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: Base 58730a15 used `() => ...` callback replacers, which bypass $-substitution; head passes plain strings, so GetSubstitution expands `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched token (`{{PATCH}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`), `$'`→everything after the placeholder in critic.md (duplicating the template tail into the middle of the patch), and `` $` ``→everything before it. bundle.patch is a raw git diff of arbitrary code (read at line 33), and diffs containing `$$` (Makefiles/shell: `kill $$`, `$$VAR`), `$&`, `$'`, or `` $` `` are common; JSON.stringify does not escape `$`. Result: the critic reviews a mangled patch and a prompt with duplicated instruction text, producing corrupted findings/verdict for exactly those PRs — a regression introduced by this change, not pre-existing behavior.

findings.title: Restore callback replacer so $ patterns in bundle JSON survive
findings.whyItBreaks: Same regression at the first call site: base wrapped `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` in `() => ...`; head passes the string directly, so any `$$`/`$&`/`$'`/`` $` `` inside the serialized bundle — which includes bundle.patch itself and any quoted diff/finding text — is expanded during `.replace("{{BUNDLE}}", ...)`. `$'`/`` $` `` splice the surrounding review.md template text into the middle of the JSON block and `$$` silently becomes `$`, so the first runCodex call (line 28) receives a corrupted bundle: the reviewer analyzes altered patch content and malformed JSON, and any findings derived from it are wrong for those inputs.
